newsitem.title: GREECE: Ecu/drachma ignores poor C/A deficit figure,ranges.
newsitem.headline: Ecu/drachma ignores poor C/A deficit figure,ranges.

text.p: Ecu/drachma steadied at lower levels, just below 304, shrugging off a 41 percent jump in the cumulative January-October 1996 current account deficit to $4.3 billion, dealers said.

"The market is bullish on the drachma and it shows even in days when poor economic figures come out," said a forex dealer at a foreign bank. "The hard rock drachma has burst last week's speculative selling of drachmas for ecus from London-based banks setting a cap in the process."
He echoed others who foresee more gains for the drachma versus the ecu in the near-term on the back of a favourable macroeconomic environment.
Ecu/drachma was trading around 303.93/03 at 1335 GMT.
"It is obvious that the market puts less weight on the balance of payments," he said. "When you look at it item by item and take into account speedier economic growth you feel better."
The disappointing current account deficit in the first eight months of 1996 reflected a larger trade deficit and a smaller invisibles surplus, Bank of Greece said.

Stronger imports of capital goods by private firms and administrative problems with the absorption of EU funds bear the lion's share in the blame for the wider current account deficit, economists said.
Greek GDP growth is estimated at 2.6 percent in 1996 and is projected to accelerate to 3.3 percent in 1997.

"The effect of the strong drachma on the competitiveness of Greek goods and services is limited and accounts for nearly one-third or less of the additional trade deficit of $952 million in January-October," said a senior economist at a foreign bank.
The strong drachma has been credited for the slowdown of inflation to 6.8 percent year-on-year in January from 7.3 percent in December.

"One should not forget that the healthy drachma has put a lid on the prices of imported raw materials and other goods that go into the production process, contain the borrowing costs of Greek firms and lead to more reasonable collective bargaining," he said.
The forex reserves were rising steadily in the last few months standing at $20.5 billion at the end of December, the central bank said. --Dimitris Kontogiannis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
